open_obligations: Check that Kenton et al.'s QuALITY subset is comparable in difficulty to Khan et al.'s HARD subset.
Note different debater models (Gemini Pro 1.5 versus GPT-4-Turbo) and judges.
Check whether Kenton et al. use a quote verification tool.
in.other_title: Extractive QA with information asymmetry: debate beats consultancy and QA without article
in.rationale: Khan et al. report non-expert LLM judges reach 76% with debate versus 54% with consultancy on QuALITY HARD. Kenton et al. report that on extractive tasks (QuALITY, BoolQ, GPQA-extractive) where only debaters see the article, judges are more accurate under debate than consultancy, except the weakest judge Gemma7B; both use LLM debaters with privileged article access.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: whether debate beats consultancy for non-expert LLM judges on information-asymmetric reading comprehension

open_obligations: Recompute ASD for Khan et al.'s consultancy runs (both correct and incorrect assignments were run).
Check that Khan et al.'s debates meet Sudhir et al.'s definition of simultaneous debate.
Check whether the debate-over-consultancy ordering survives under ASD.
in.other_title: Agent score difference (ASD) replaces judge accuracy as the protocol metric
in.rationale: Khan et al. report judge accuracy of 88% (humans) and 76% (LLMs) with debate versus 78% and 54% with consultancy. Sudhir et al. argue that judge accuracy relative to consultancy is the wrong alignment metric and that ASD, the score difference between arguing the true and false answer, is equivalent to judge accuracy for simultaneous debate but not for consultancy; Khan et al.'s debates are simultaneous, so only the consultancy side of the comparison is affected.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate's judge-accuracy gain over consultancy measures how much a protocol rewards truth-telling

open_obligations: Check that 'QA without article' matches Khan et al.'s 'Naive' baseline (the authors say it does on p7)
Confirm the Gemma7B exception and the closed-task debate-vs-QA results are not counted as support
in.other_title: Kenton et al. find Khan et al.'s debate-over-consultancy QuALITY result generalises to other tasks
in.rationale: Khan et al. report debate beats consultancy and naive (no-article) judging on QuALITY; the authors explicitly say these results generalise to further extractive tasks and, for debate vs consultancy, to closed tasks. Differences: different models, inference-only, and debate does not beat QA with article.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Judge accuracy of debate vs consultancy and vs QA without article, for judges weaker than or equal to the debaters

open_obligations: Note that the capability gap is information access, which Khan et al. list as a limitation.
Check whether ground truth is used only for evaluation, as sandwiching requires.
Note that no model is aligned in an inner loop.
out.other_title: Do debate, market-making and recursive reward modeling work in sandwiching trials?
out.rationale: Bowman et al. ask whether debate can be validated empirically under sandwiching. Khan et al. report non-expert human judges reach 88% with LLM debate versus 60% naive and 78% consultancy, with GPT-4-Turbo debaters who can read the story; the experts are LLMs with privileged information rather than more capable models, and no fine-tuning is done by the non-experts.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate between LLMs helps non-expert judges beyond a baseline, in a hidden-passage QuALITY HARD setup

open_obligations: Note the different information condition: Khan et al.'s judges see no passage, Parrish et al.'s have 90 s of access.
Check that the naive baseline (60%) is comparable to Parrish et al.'s passage-only condition.
Check the human judge filtering (21 judges after filtering) for selection effects.
out.other_title: Single-turn debate null result is a limited case study, not evidence against debate
out.rationale: Parrish et al. say their null result is a limited case study, not evidence against debate. Khan et al. report non-expert human judges reach 88% with debate between persuasive LLM debaters versus 60% naive and 78% consultancy on QuALITY HARD; their judges cannot read the story and see verified quotes, and debates run for 3 rounds.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether a debate set-up can help non-expert judges on QuALITY when the single-turn human-argument null result is not the whole story

open_obligations: Check whether Parrish et al.'s snippet (PS) baseline is the right analogue of Khan et al.'s naive baseline.
Note the difference between human-written single-turn arguments and multi-round LLM debate.
Check judge selection: 21 filtered judges versus 194 MTurk workers.
out.other_title: Single-turn debate-style arguments do not improve human accuracy on hard QuALITY questions
out.rationale: Parrish et al. report human-written single-turn arguments did not improve time-limited judges' accuracy. Khan et al. report non-expert human judges reach 88% with 3-round LLM debate versus 60% naive on QuALITY HARD; Khan et al.'s judges cannot read the story and see verified quotes, while Parrish et al.'s have 90 s of passage access and snippets, so the null and positive results come from different information conditions.
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate-style arguments improve accuracy of non-expert judges on hard QuALITY questions

open_obligations: Note Michael et al.'s GPT-4 result did not show the gap, so debater strength matters.
Check that judge pools and training are comparable.
Check that both use the QuALITY HARD (Gutenberg) questions.
out.other_title: Judge accuracy: human debate 84%, human consultancy 74%, AI debate 78%, AI consultancy 80%
out.rationale: Michael et al. report human-judge accuracy of 84% for human debate versus 74% for human consultancy, with GPT-4 debate at 78% and consultancy at 80%. Khan et al. report 88% for debate versus 78% for consultancy with optimised GPT-4-Turbo debaters, so with stronger LLM debaters the debate-over-consultancy gap Michael et al. saw with human debaters appears for AI debaters too; Khan et al. use fixed rounds.
out.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: whether debate gives non-expert human judges higher accuracy than consultancy on QuALITY HARD with a hidden passage

text: For the most persuasive models, the paper reports non-expert human judges achieve 88% and non-expert LLM judges 76% accuracy with debate, where naive (no-expert) performance is 60% and 48%. With the single-model consultancy baseline, human and LLM judges achieve 78% and 54%.
title: Human judges 88% with debate vs 78% consultancy; LLM judges 76% vs 54% (naive 60% / 48%)
